---
title: "Simulation as a method"
subtitle: "Synthetic data with a known recipe"
bibliography: [../references.bib, ../references-new.bib]
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
set.seed(20260731)

# The simulated twin, the panel that it
# reproduces, and the files that the generator, its validation and the null
# multiverse write
sim   <- readr::read_csv("../cases/eu-frames/data/EUframes_person_full.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
panel <- readr::read_csv("../cases/eu-frames/data/EUframes_cy.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
sweep <- readr::read_csv("_model-outputs/sim_recovery_joint.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
valid <- readr::read_csv("_model-outputs/twin_validation.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
null_mv <- readr::read_csv("_model-outputs/sim_null_multiverse.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

DIMS <- c("cosmo", "util", "comm", "lib")

# The specification that the twin reproduces at cell level: C6HJR's published Multi100 specification
# with a growth co-predictor, one step along the co-predictor fork.
c6hjr_terms <- c("unemp", "growth", "factor(year)", "factor(cntry)")

# What the recipe plants at cell level is the coefficient of the panel itself,
# because the generator solves each country-year's item thresholds until its
# expected dimension means ARE those in the panel. Computed here rather than
# read from a file, so it cannot go stale against the panel it comes from.
planted <- purrr::map(c(DIMS, "pos", "neg"), \(v) {
  cf <- coef(lm(reformulate(c6hjr_terms, response = paste0("m", v)), data = panel))
  tibble::tibble(outcome = v, planted_unemp = cf[["unemp"]],
         planted_growth = cf[["growth"]])
}) |> purrr::list_rbind()

sim_cells <- sim |>
  dplyr::summarise(dplyr::across(c(dplyr::all_of(DIMS), pos, neg), mean),
            unemp = dplyr::first(unemp), growth = dplyr::first(growth),
            .by = c(cntry, year))
```

This is the simulation module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd), and it is optional. Most quantitative pages on this site analyse data that came from the world; this module analyses data that came from a recipe written in advance, so that the answer is known before any model runs. That inversion, known as fake-data simulation, is a standard habit in applied statistics. *Regression and Other Stories* uses it constantly, on the argument that fitting models to data whose coefficients you planted yourself is how you learn what your models can and cannot recover [@GelmanEtAl2020RegressionOtherStories]. The same habit underpins classroom practice [@GelmanVehtari2024ActiveStatisticsStories] and the workflow literature, where experimentation on simulated data is one of the named components of model-building [@GelmanEtAl2026BayesianWorkflow].

The module works on the simulated twin of the EU-frames case, a person-level file built from a recipe, for the two things that only it can show: how composition and context can be told apart, and what a multiverse of estimators finds in a world with nothing to find. It belongs with the [individual-level module](individual-level.qmd) and with [stage 4](../tracks/self-study/stage-4.qmd) of the self-study route.

The null world of section 3 is declared and diagnosed with DeclareDesign [@BlairEtAl2023DeclareDesignDeclareDiagnose], an R package that describes a research design in four parts, which its authors call the model, the inquiry, the data strategy and the answer strategy. The **model** is the recipe, the description of the units and of how each would respond to each condition. The **inquiry** is the quantity that the study is meant to learn, its estimand. The **data strategy** says how the units are sampled and assigned, and the **answer strategy** is the estimator. Declared that way, a design can be run as often as one likes, and the package summarises the runs: how far the estimates fall from the estimand on average, how widely they scatter, how often the interval covers the truth, and how often the test rejects. The simulations with many draws ran once, in scripts in `companion/_model-outputs/` of the source repository, and the page reads their results.

## 1. The simulated twin {#sec-dgp}

The EU-frames case rests on Eurobarometer microdata that GESIS licenses and that cannot be redistributed in any form, including as samples or extracts ([the data sources module](data-sources.qmd#sec-gesis) explains that regime). The course therefore ships a synthetic person-level companion to its country-year panel, `EUframes_person_full.csv`: `r format(nrow(sim), big.mark = ",")` synthetic respondents across the real 270 country-year cells, with the real macro variables attached, the four framing dimensions and both composites, and every individual variable that the original author (OA) of the case used. No Eurobarometer respondent appears in it. What the licensed file supplied, read once and locally, is a set of aggregate statistics of the kind that published appendices report – marginal distributions, a correlation matrix and the coefficients of a model of the survey instrument – committed as `_model-outputs/joint_*.csv` and `_model-outputs/item_*.csv`.

The generator, `_model-outputs/simulate_person_joint.R`, works in two stages. In the first, a respondent's characteristics are one draw from a latent multivariate normal distribution whose correlation matrix was estimated on the real respondents, and each observed variable is a monotone transform of one coordinate of that draw, so that every marginal distribution and every pairwise association is reproduced. In the second, the generator simulates the survey instrument rather than the four scores. A respondent hears a list of thirteen things that the EU might mean and names those that apply, and each item has a latent propensity

$$
z_{ij} = \alpha_{j(ct)} + \mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol\beta_j + \varepsilon_{ij},
\qquad \text{item } j \text{ mentioned when } z_{ij} > 0,
$$

with $\mathbf{x}_i$ the characteristics of respondent $i$, $\alpha_{j(ct)}$ a shift for their country-year, and the thirteen residuals correlated with one another. That is a **multivariate probit**, a set of probit equations, one per item, whose error terms are allowed to correlate. For each of the 270 country-years the generator solves the shifts by Newton iteration, a numerical search that corrects a guess step by step, until the expected dimension means match those in the panel.

The licence of the twin to be used is its validation. The same model was fitted to the real respondents and to the twin, and the coefficients were compared:

```{r}
#| label: validation-summary
valid |>
  datawizard::data_summary(coefficients = length(z),
                           within_1_se = sum(abs(z) < 1),
                           within_2_se = sum(abs(z) < 2),
                           largest = round(max(abs(z)), 2))
```

`r sum(abs(valid$z) < 2)` of `r nrow(valid)` coefficients agree within two standard errors of the difference, the scale that asks whether a gap exceeds the sampling noise of the twin itself, and `r sum(abs(valid$gap_in_se) < 2)` on the far stricter scale of the standard error of the real fit, which a file a tenth of the size cannot meet. The same comparison caught two failures of earlier versions of the generator, and nothing else would have caught them. The first left occupation out of the answer stage, so that a model with occupation and education split the association between them differently from the real data while every marginal, every cell mean and every correlation checked out. The second treated education as a straight line where the published model reads three bands, and returned about half of each band contrast. The [individual-level module](individual-level.qmd#sec-twin) reads the validated coefficients.

The cell means of the twin carry one known bias, which no single draw reveals. Each cell mean is an average over a tenth of the real respondents, so a model fitted to the cell means of one draw lands near the coefficient of the panel without matching it, and only repeated draws from the same recipe show whether the misses are noise. @fig-sweep shows independent draws, each refitted with the specification of C6HJR with growth beside unemployment.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sweep
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "Independent draws from the recipe of the twin, each refitted at cell level with C6HJR's published Multi100 specification and growth beside unemployment. Red marks show the coefficient of the panel, which the recipe plants. The unemployment slopes sit consistently outside their marks. Source: `companion/_model-outputs/sim_recovery_joint.csv`."
ggplot2::ggplot(sweep, ggplot2::aes(sim_unemp, outcome)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.45, colour = "#00205b", size = 1.6) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(data = planted, ggplot2::aes(planted_unemp, outcome),
             colour = "#c8102e", shape = 124, size = 8) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "estimated unemployment slope", y = NULL) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

```{r}
#| label: sweep-summary
#| include: false
sweep_unemp <- sweep |>
  datawizard::data_summary(mean_estimate = mean(sim_unemp), by = "outcome") |>
  dplyr::left_join(planted, by = "outcome")
one_draw <- sim_cells |>
  dplyr::left_join(panel |> datawizard::data_select(select = c("cntry", "year", "mcosmo")),
                   by = c("cntry", "year")) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(diff = cosmo - mcosmo)
one_draw_t <- lm(reformulate(c6hjr_terms, response = "diff"), data = one_draw) |>
  parameters::model_parameters(keep = "^unemp$")
```

Every unemployment slope misses in the same direction, with the estimate from the twin larger in magnitude than the planted value by `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * (stats::median(abs(sweep_unemp$mean_estimate) / abs(sweep_unemp$planted_unemp)) - 1))` per cent at the median over the six outcomes. Regressing the difference between the cell means of the committed twin and those of the panel on the same specification gives an unemployment coefficient with t = `r insight::format_value(one_draw_t$t, digits = 2, style_negative = "minus")`, indistinguishable from zero, so that one draw cannot separate the bias from its own noise. The source is a known limitation of the construction: the generator gives each country-year one shift per dimension where the real data has one rate per item. The obvious repair, a separate rate for each of the thirteen items in each cell, makes the marginals exact and the individual-level validation worse, because the twin draws its people from pooled marginals and a forced rate pushes the difference into the coefficients of the individual variables. The twin is therefore validated for the individual-level model and biased by about a sixth for slopes of unemployment on cell means, and the bias is documented rather than removed.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Open the generator and change `SIM_FRACTION` from `0.10` to `0.40`. That setting alone decides how many respondents each cell gets, so the only thing that changes is how precisely a cell mean can be measured. Judge the result over several draws, not one: ten seeds at each setting, with `$SIM_SEED` naming the draw and `$SIM_SWEEP` collecting the estimates, and compare the standard deviations of the two sets of ten. Quadrupling the cell sizes should roughly halve them, because the standard error of a mean falls with the square root of the sample size. Point `$SIM_OUT` at a scratch directory unless you mean to overwrite the committed twin, and note that at `0.40` the file is four times the size.
:::

## 2. Composition against context {#sec-composition}

The unemployment rate of a country-year could move EU framing in two ways. It might be that unemployed *people* frame the EU differently, so that a high-unemployment cell holds more of them and its mean shifts with the mix, a **compositional** effect. Or living through high unemployment might change how everyone frames the EU, whatever their own situation, a **contextual** effect.

The country-year panel cannot separate them, because it contains no individuals. The twin can, because it carries a calibrated occupational structure: being unemployed has its own estimated effect on what a respondent says, and the share of the respondents of a cell who are unemployed rises with the national rate by a measured amount. Both halves matter, and the second is usually assumed rather than measured. A large individual effect spread over a group that barely grows moves an average hardly at all, and the arithmetic that combines the two is more informative than either coefficient alone. The [individual-level module](individual-level.qmd#sec-composition) does that calculation on the twin and finds that the compositional path accounts for a few per cent of the country-level association.

An earlier version of this twin manufactured the compositional channel. It gave respondents an invented unemployment indicator whose prevalence was a fixed multiple of the national rate, so that this section would have something to display. Nothing about it was measured, since the prevalence rule and the effect were both chosen, and it fused two constructs that belong to different levels, the unemployment rate of a labour market and the employment status of a person. **A simulation can demonstrate only what was put into it.** If the mechanism on display is one that you programmed into the generator yourself, the demonstration establishes that your code works, and nothing about the world. Simulated data can check whether an estimator recovers an answer, as section 3 does for an answer of zero, but they cannot supply the answer.

## 3. A null world {#sec-null}

The [inference reading](../cases/eu-frames/reading-inference.qmd) of the EU-frames case argues that to test a specification curve one must know what the curve would look like if there were nothing to find, and the test designed there builds that null distribution by permutation. Simulation offers a more direct route: write the recipe with the effect removed and record what the estimators find. The script `simulate_null_multiverse.R` declares such a world with DeclareDesign. It keeps the 270 cells of the panel with their unemployment rates, gives each cell a tenth of its real respondents as the twin does, and draws a country effect, a country-year effect and a person-level score whose spreads come from the panel and the twin (`r insight::format_value(null_mv$sd_country[1], digits = 3)`, `r insight::format_value(null_mv$sd_cell[1], digits = 3)` and `r insight::format_value(null_mv$sd_person[1], digits = 3)`), with unemployment given no effect at all. Four estimators that the course discusses are fitted to each of `r null_mv$n_sims[1]` draws, and the share of draws in which each rejects the true value of zero at the 5% level is its rate of false positives.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-null
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Four estimators in a world in which unemployment has no effect: the share of 500 simulated datasets in which each rejected a slope of zero at the 5% level, with the simulation error of that share (a bootstrap over the draws), and the spread of the estimates. Source: `companion/_model-outputs/sim_null_multiverse.csv`."
null_mv |>
  datawizard::data_modify(estimator = factor(estimator, c("pooled", "country_re", "three_level", "cell_means"))) |>
  datawizard::data_arrange("estimator") |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    Estimator = c(pooled = "OLS on respondents, clustering ignored",
                  country_re = "random intercepts for countries",
                  three_level = "random intercepts for countries and country-years",
                  cell_means = "OLS on the 270 cell means")[as.character(estimator)],
    `False positives` = insight::format_value(rejection_rate, as_percent = TRUE, digits = 1),
    `Simulation error` = insight::format_value(rejection_rate_se, as_percent = TRUE, digits = 1),
    `SD of the estimates` = insight::format_value(sd_estimate, digits = 5)
  ) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 2:4, align = "r")
```

Every row estimates a quantity known to be zero, and none of the four is biased, since nothing in the recipe ties unemployment to anything. The rows differ in the uncertainty that they attach to their estimates, and so in how often they claim an effect. The regression on respondents that ignores their clustering treats forty thousand respondents as independent pieces of evidence about a predictor that takes 270 values, and it rejects in `r insight::format_value(null_mv$rejection_rate[null_mv$estimator == "pooled"], as_percent = TRUE, digits = 0)` of the draws. Random intercepts for countries alone still count every respondent of a country-year as new evidence about its unemployment rate, and reject in `r insight::format_value(null_mv$rejection_rate[null_mv$estimator == "country_re"], as_percent = TRUE, digits = 0)`. The regression on the 270 cell means counts cells rather than respondents, but it treats the ten cells of a country as independent although they share the effect of their country, and it rejects in `r insight::format_value(null_mv$rejection_rate[null_mv$estimator == "cell_means"], as_percent = TRUE, digits = 0)`, the error that [section 3 of the statistics module](stats-methods.qmd#sec-pooled) corrects by clustering the errors by country. Only the model that declares both levels, the countries and the country-years, comes close to the 5% that a valid test should deliver, at `r insight::format_value(null_mv$rejection_rate[null_mv$estimator == "three_level"], as_percent = TRUE, digits = 1)` with a simulation error of `r insight::format_value(100 * null_mv$rejection_rate_se[null_mv$estimator == "three_level"], digits = 1)` percentage points. The two multilevel estimators also scatter about half as widely as the two regressions, because they draw on the comparisons within countries, so the model that gets the uncertainty right is also the more precise one here. The [statistics module](stats-methods.qmd#sec-multilevel) shows the same contrast in the degrees of freedom of the fits on the real respondents.

A multiverse of four estimators fitted to a null world shows on a small scale what a full permutation test constructs, the distribution of whole curves when the true effect is zero. It also constrains how the percentages of the real curve should be read, a point that [the multiverse module](multiverse.qmd#sec-reading) develops. Some share of any set of specifications will look supportive under a true zero, and a set that includes estimators which overstate the evidence will look supportive much more often, so a share on its own, without a null distribution to compare it with, cannot show that the curve differs from what a true zero would produce.

```{r}
#| label: fig-lineup
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "A lineup: nine cell-level scatters of mean simulated cosmopolitan framing against unemployment. Eight permute the unemployment series within country; one is the real structure of the twin. Pick the panel that looks like an effect before reading on."
real_panel <- sample(1:9, 1)
purrr::map(1:9, \(i) {
  d <- if (i == real_panel) sim_cells else
    sim_cells |> dplyr::mutate(unemp = sample(unemp), .by = cntry)
  d |> dplyr::mutate(panel = i)
}) |>
  purrr::list_rbind() |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(unemp, cosmo)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 0.8, colour = "#00205b") +
  ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.6, colour = "#c8102e") +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~panel) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "unemployment (%)", y = "cell mean, simulated cosmopolitan share") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

```{r}
#| label: lineup-answer
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cat(sprintf("::: {.callout-note collapse=\"true\"}\n## Which panel is real?\nPanel %d. If you picked it, you have informally rejected the null by eye, which is the logic of a permutation test applied visually. If you could not, that is itself evidence about how strong a level-2 relationship of this size looks at this sample size.\n:::\n", real_panel))  # r-style: keep – output: asis writes this callout into the page
```

## Further reading {#sec-further}

For the habit itself, *Regression and Other Stories* is the core text, with short fake-data simulations that recur throughout and build on one another [@GelmanEtAl2020RegressionOtherStories], and *Active Statistics* packages the same moves as classroom activities [@GelmanVehtari2024ActiveStatisticsStories]. For declaring a design before the data exist and diagnosing it by simulation, the documentation of DeclareDesign works through experiments, surveys and observational designs in the four parts set out at the top of this page [@BlairEtAl2023DeclareDesignDeclareDiagnose]. For multilevel structures, DeBruine and Barr build a mixed-effects simulation from nothing and recover its parameters, on the argument that constructing the data is how you come to understand the model [@DeBruineBarr2021UnderstandingMixedeffectsModels]. For simulation inside a modelling workflow – prior and posterior predictive checking, calibration, experimentation on synthetic data before touching the real thing – the Bayesian workflow book is the current statement [@GelmanEtAl2026BayesianWorkflow], and its habits transfer well beyond Bayesian settings. And for simulation as a research method in its own right, the design framework of @MorrisEtAl2019UsingSimulationStudies supplies the vocabulary (aims, data-generating mechanisms, estimands, methods and performance measures, stated before the study is run), the book-length treatment written for social scientists is @CarseyHarden2014MonteCarloSimulation, and an applied Monte Carlo study on cross-lagged panel models shows the method applied to a question close to the choice of estimator in the EU-frames case [@LeszczenskyWolbring2022HowDealReverse].

Simulation studies are analyses too, and they have researcher degrees of freedom of their own – conditions, performance measures, which results get reported – so a comparative study can be tuned until any method looks superior [@PawelEtAl2024PitfallsPotentialsSimulation]. The disciplines that this course keeps returning to, preregistered designs and justified choices, apply to simulated data as much as to real data. The script of the null world, the generator of the twin and its calibration are all committed, so the quickest place to begin is the Try it of section 1: change the recipe, run it again, and check what the estimator does when you already know the answer.
